title: Integration I: the definite integral and substitution

problems.html: Estimate the area under f(x)=x2f(x)=x^{2}f(x)=x2 on [0,2][0,2][0,2] using n=4n=4n=4 rectangles of equal width and the height at the right end of each strip. Is your estimate an over- or under-estimate, and why?
hints: The strip width is the interval length divided by the number of strips, so δx=2−04\delta x=\tfrac{2-0}{4}δx=42−0​.
Right-endpoint means the height of each rectangle is fff evaluated at the right-hand edge: x=0.5,1,1.5,2x=0.5,1,1.5,2x=0.5,1,1.5,2.
For the over/under question, ask where in each strip the function is largest. For an increasing function the right edge is the tallest point, so every rectangle pokes above the curve.
problems.format: the estimate, then over or under

problems.html: Without computing any antiderivative, decide the sign (positive, negative or zero) of each definite integral, and say why. (a) ∫−22x3  dx,(b) ∫01e−x  dx,(c) ∫π2πsin⁡x  dx.\text{(a)}\ \int_{-2}^{2} x^{3}\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ \int_{0}^{1} \mathrm{e}^{-x}\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\ \int_{\pi}^{2\pi}\sin x\,\,\mathrm{d}x.(a) ∫−22​x3dx,(b) ∫01​e−xdx,(c) ∫π2π​sinxdx.
hints: You are being asked about signed area, so the question is whether the graph sits above or below the axis on the given interval.
In (a) the integrand is odd and the interval is symmetric about the origin — the two halves cancel exactly.
In (b) an exponential is positive everywhere; in (c) sine is below the axis throughout the second half of its period.
problems.format: (a), (b), (c): the value or the sign

problems.html:
A picture first.

  1. Sketch y=x2y=x^{2}y=x2 on [0,2][0,2][0,2] and, on the same axes, draw the four right-endpoint Riemann rectangles of Exercise 1 (width 0.50.50.5). Mark whether the rectangles lie above or below the curve.

  2. On separate axes sketch g(x)=x−1g(x)=x-1g(x)=x−1 on [0,2][0,2][0,2]. Shade the region between the graph and the xxx-axis, marking the part that counts as negative signed area. Then compute the net signed area ∫02(x−1)  dx\int_0^2 (x-1)\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫02​(x−1)dx and the total (unsigned) area.
hints: In (a) each rectangle's top-right corner sits on the curve, so compare rectangle and curve within each strip.
In (b) the line crosses the axis at x=1x=1x=1, splitting the region into two triangles — one below the axis and one above.
Signed area counts the part below the axis as negative; total area counts it as positive. Compute the two triangles and combine them each way.
problems.format: the signed area, then the total area

problems.html: Suppose ∫02f=5\displaystyle\int_0^2 f=5∫02​f=5 and ∫25f=−2\displaystyle\int_2^5 f=-2∫25​f=−2. Using only the properties of the definite integral (do not find fff), evaluate (a)∫05f,(b)∫52f,(c)∫22f,(d)∫023f,(e)∫50f.\text{(a)}\int_0^5 f,\quad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\int_5^2 f,\quad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\int_2^2 f,\quad\allowbreak \text{(d)}\int_0^2 3f,\quad\allowbreak \text{(e)}\int_5^0 f.(a)∫05​f,(b)∫52​f,(c)∫22​f,(d)∫02​3f,(e)∫50​f.
hints: Do not try to find fff — every part follows from one of the standard properties.
Adjacent intervals add: ∫05=∫02+∫25\int_0^5=\int_0^2+\int_2^5∫05​=∫02​+∫25​. Reversing the limits flips the sign, and equal limits give zero.
A constant factor comes straight out of the integral, so (d) is three times a value you already have.
problems.format: (a)–(e), comma-separated

problems.html: Find ∫(x3−4x+2)  dx\displaystyle\int\bigl(x^{3}-4x+2\bigr)\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫(x3−4x+2)dx.
hints: Integrate term by term, reversing the power rule: raise the exponent by one and divide by the new exponent.
The constant term 222 integrates to 2x2x2x, since it is 2x02x^02x0.
Check your answer by differentiating it — that should return the original integrand exactly.
problems.format: the antiderivative at x = 1, taking C = 0

problems.html: Write each integrand as a power of xxx first: ∫(x+1x2)  dx\displaystyle\int\Bigl(\sqrt{x}+\frac{1}{x^{2}}\Bigr)\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫(x​+x21​)dx.
hints: Rewrite both terms as powers of xxx before doing anything else: x=x1/2\sqrt x=x^{1/2}x​=x1/2 and 1x2=x−2\dfrac{1}{x^2}=x^{-2}x21​=x−2.
Now the power rule applies to each. Note it works perfectly well for negative and fractional exponents.
The one exponent it cannot handle is −1-1−1, and that does not occur here — but x−2x^{-2}x−2 integrates to x−1/(−1)x^{-1}/(-1)x−1/(−1), so watch the sign.
problems.format: the antiderivative at x = 1, with C = 0

problems.html: Use the table of standard integrals: ∫(2ex−3x+5cos⁡x)  dx\displaystyle\int\Bigl(2\mathrm{e}^{x}-\frac{3}{x}+5\cos x\Bigr)\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫(2ex−x3​+5cosx)dx.
hints: Each term is a standard integral; constants come out in front and the three pieces are independent.
The middle term is the exception to the power rule: ∫1x dx=ln⁡∣x∣\int\dfrac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x=\ln|x|∫x1​dx=ln∣x∣, with the modulus.
Watch the sign on the last term: the integral of cos⁡\coscos is +sin⁡+\sin+sin, whereas the derivative of cos⁡\coscos is −sin⁡-\sin−sin.
problems.format: the antiderivative at x = 1 (C = 0), to 3 d.p.

problems.html: Evaluate the indefinite integrals (a)∫e3x  dx,(b)∫sec⁡2(2x)  dx,(c)∫ dx9+x2,(d)∫ dx4−x2,(e)∫cos⁡(5x)  dx.\text{(a)}\int\mathrm{e}^{3x}\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\quad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\int\sec^{2}(2x)\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\quad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\int\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{9+x^{2}},\quad\allowbreak \text{(d)}\int\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{\sqrt{4-x^{2}}},\quad\allowbreak \text{(e)}\int\cos(5x)\,\,\mathrm{d}x.(a)∫e3xdx,(b)∫sec2(2x)dx,(c)∫9+x2dx​,(d)∫4−x2​dx​,(e)∫cos(5x)dx.
hints: Each is a table integral, but with the variable scaled — so a compensating constant appears out front.
The rule is: if ∫f(x) dx=F(x)\int f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=F(x)∫f(x)dx=F(x) then ∫f(ax) dx=1aF(ax)\int f(ax)\,\mathrm{d}x=\tfrac1a F(ax)∫f(ax)dx=a1​F(ax). That covers (a), (b) and (e).

For (c) and (d) match the pattern to the table with the right aaa: ∫dxa2+x2=1aarctan⁡xa\int\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{a^2+x^2}=\dfrac1a\arctan\dfrac{x}{a}∫a2+x2dx​=a1​arctanax​, and ∫dxa2−x2=arcsin⁡xa\int\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}=\arcsin\dfrac{x}{a}∫a2−x2​dx​=arcsinax​ with no constant at all.
problems.format: the constant in front of each of (a)–(e)

problems.html: Evaluate (a)∫13x2  dx,(b)∫0π/2cos⁡x  dx,(c)∫1e dxx,(d)∫01e2x  dx.\text{(a)}\int_{1}^{3} x^{2}\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos x\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\int_{1}^{\mathrm{e}}\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{x},\qquad\allowbreak \text{(d)}\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{e}^{2x}\,\,\mathrm{d}x.(a)∫13​x2dx,(b)∫0π/2​cosxdx,(c)∫1e​xdx​,(d)∫01​e2xdx.
hints: Find any antiderivative, then evaluate it at the top limit and subtract its value at the bottom.
The constant of integration is unnecessary here: it appears in both terms and cancels in the subtraction.
In (c) the antiderivative is ln⁡x\ln xlnx, and ln⁡e=1\ln\mathrm{e}=1lne=1; in (d) remember the 12\tfrac1221​ from integrating e2x\mathrm{e}^{2x}e2x.
problems.format: (a)–(c) exact; then (d) to 3 d.p.

problems.html: Differentiate with respect to xxx (do not try to evaluate the integral): (a)  d dx∫0xe−t2  dt,(b)  d dx∫2xsin⁡(t3)  dt,(c)  d dx∫1x dt1+t4.\text{(a)}\ \frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}x}\int_{0}^{x}\mathrm{e}^{-t^{2}}\,\,\mathrm{d}t,\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ \frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}x}\int_{2}^{x}\sin(t^{3})\,\,\mathrm{d}t,\qquad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\ \frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}x}\int_{1}^{x}\frac{\,\mathrm{d}t}{1+t^{4}}.(a) dxd​∫0x​e−t2dt,(b) dxd​∫2x​sin(t3)dt,(c) dxd​∫1x​1+t4dt​.
hints: This is the first part of the fundamental theorem, and it needs no integration at all.
Differentiating an integral with respect to its upper limit simply returns the integrand, with the limit substituted for the dummy variable.
So replace ttt by xxx in each integrand and stop. Notice that (a) and (b) have no elementary antiderivative, yet their derivatives are immediate.
problems.format: (a) and (b) at x = 1, to 3 d.p.

problems.html: Each integrand contains an “inside” function whose derivative is present. Integrate by substitution: (a)∫2x (x2+1)5  dx,(b)∫cos⁡x esin⁡x  dx,(c)∫3x2 (x3+7)4  dx.\text{(a)}\int 2x\,(x^{2}+1)^{5}\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\quad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\int \cos x\,\mathrm{e}^{\sin x}\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\quad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\int 3x^{2}\,(x^{3}+7)^{4}\,\,\mathrm{d}x.(a)∫2x(x2+1)5dx,(b)∫cosxesinxdx,(c)∫3x2(x3+7)4dx.
hints: Look for an inner function whose derivative is also present as a factor — that is the signal for substitution.
In (a) put u=x2+1u=x^2+1u=x2+1, so du=2x dx\mathrm{d}u=2x\,\mathrm{d}xdu=2xdx and the whole 2x2x2x is absorbed, leaving ∫u5 du\int u^5\,\mathrm{d}u∫u5du.
Do the same in (b) with u=sin⁡xu=\sin xu=sinx and in (c) with u=x3+7u=x^3+7u=x3+7. Always convert back to xxx at the end.
problems.format: the constant in front of each of (a)–(c)

problems.html: Spot the f′/ff'/ff′/f pattern and write down the logarithm: (a)∫2xx2+5  dx,(b)∫cos⁡xsin⁡x  dx,(c)∫exex+1  dx.\text{(a)}\int\frac{2x}{x^{2}+5}\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\int\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\int\frac{\mathrm{e}^{x}}{\mathrm{e}^{x}+1}\,\,\mathrm{d}x.(a)∫x2+52x​dx,(b)∫sinxcosx​dx,(c)∫ex+1ex​dx.
hints: Each of these is the special case where the numerator is exactly the derivative of the denominator.
That pattern integrates to a logarithm: ∫g′g dx=ln⁡∣g∣+C\int\dfrac{g'}{g}\,\mathrm{d}x=\ln|g|+C∫gg′​dx=ln∣g∣+C, with no extra constant needed.
Check each: in (a) the derivative of x2+5x^2+5x2+5 is 2x2x2x; in (b) the derivative of sin⁡x\sin xsinx is cos⁡x\cos xcosx; in (c) the derivative of ex+1\mathrm{e}^{x}+1ex+1 is ex\mathrm{e}^{x}ex.
problems.format: (a) and (c) at x = 0 (C = 0), to 3 d.p.

problems.html: Evaluate ∫01x ex2  dx\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} x\,\mathrm{e}^{x^{2}}\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫01​xex2dx by changing the limits to the new variable.
hints: Substitute u=x2u=x^2u=x2, so du=2x dx\mathrm{d}u=2x\,\mathrm{d}xdu=2xdx and the xxx already present supplies half of it.
Because the integral is definite, convert the limits too: x=0x=0x=0 gives u=0u=0u=0 and x=1x=1x=1 gives u=1u=1u=1.
Once the limits are in terms of uuu there is no need to substitute back — evaluate directly in uuu.
problems.format: the value of the integral, to 3 d.p.

problems.html: For each function, state whether it has an elementary antiderivative. (a) e−x2,(b) x e−x2,(c) sin⁡xx,(d) sin⁡(x2),(e) xcos⁡(x2).\text{(a)}\ \mathrm{e}^{-x^{2}},\quad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ x\,\mathrm{e}^{-x^{2}},\quad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\ \frac{\sin x}{x},\quad\allowbreak \text{(d)}\ \sin(x^{2}),\quad\allowbreak \text{(e)}\ x\cos(x^{2}).(a) e−x2,(b) xe−x2,(c) xsinx​,(d) sin(x2),(e) xcos(x2).
hints: The question is whether an antiderivative can be written with the usual functions at all — not whether you can find one quickly.
Look for the tell-tale extra factor: an inner function's derivative sitting alongside it makes substitution work.

In (b) the factor xxx is essentially the derivative of −x2-x^2−x2, and in (e) it is essentially the derivative of x2x^2x2. Without that factor, the integrals in (a), (c) and (d) are famously not elementary.
problems.format: (a)–(e): yes or no, comma-separated

problems.html:
▶\blacktriangleright▶ Let f(x)=1+x2f(x)=1+x^{2}f(x)=1+x2 on [0,3][0,3][0,3], cut into n=3n=3n=3 strips of width 111.

  1. Compute the right-endpoint and left-endpoint Riemann sums.

  2. Using FTC Part 2, find the exact area and check it lies between your two estimates.
hints: With width 111 and three strips, the right-endpoint heights use x=1,2,3x=1,2,3x=1,2,3 and the left-endpoint heights use x=0,1,2x=0,1,2x=0,1,2.
Compute both sums; since fff is increasing on this interval, one will overshoot and the other undershoot.
For the exact value use the fundamental theorem: integrate 1+x21+x^21+x2 and evaluate between the limits, then check it sits between your two estimates.
problems.format: left sum, right sum, then the exact value

problems.html: ▶\blacktriangleright▶ Integrate, simplifying first where it helps: (a)∫x2−3x+2x  dx,(b)∫(e2x+3x−cos⁡5x)  dx.\text{(a)}\int\frac{x^{2}-3x+2}{x}\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\int\bigl(\mathrm{e}^{2x}+\tfrac{3}{x}-\cos 5x\bigr)\,\,\mathrm{d}x .(a)∫xx2−3x+2​dx,(b)∫(e2x+x3​−cos5x)dx.
hints: In (a) divide through by xxx first — the integrand becomes three separate simple terms.
That produces a 2x\dfrac{2}{x}x2​ term, which integrates to a logarithm, not a power.
In (b) each term is a scaled standard integral, so each picks up its own compensating constant: 12\tfrac1221​, none, and 15\tfrac1551​ respectively.
problems.format: (a) exact; then (b) at x = 1 (C = 0), 3 d.p.

problems.html: (FTC evaluation — worked-example anchor.) ▶\blacktriangleright▶ Evaluate ∫24x2  dx\displaystyle\int_{2}^{4} x^{2}\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫24​x2dx and ∫01(3x2−4x+5)  dx\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\bigl(3x^{2}-4x+5\bigr)\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫01​(3x2−4x+5)dx, and state in one sentence what the first number represents geometrically.
hints: Both are direct applications of the fundamental theorem: antidifferentiate, then subtract the values at the limits.
For the first, the antiderivative of x2x^2x2 is 13x3\tfrac13x^331​x3; be careful with the arithmetic of 64−864-864−8.
For the geometric reading, note the integrand is positive throughout [2,4][2,4][2,4], so the number is a genuine area rather than a signed one.
problems.format: the two integrals, comma-separated

problems.html:
[Physics / applied] Water flows into a tank at the rate r(t)=6tr(t)=6tr(t)=6t litres per minute, 0≤t≤50\le t\le 50≤t≤5. The volume added between times aaa and bbb is ∫abr(t)  dt\int_a^b r(t)\,\,\mathrm{d}t∫ab​r(t)dt.

  1. How much water enters during the first 555 minutes?

  2. During which single minute [t,t+1][t,t+1][t,t+1] does the most water enter, and how much?
hints: A rate integrated over time gives a total, so (a) is the integral of rrr from 000 to 555.
For (b) the rate is increasing, so the busiest minute is the last one — but confirm it by comparing intervals rather than asserting it.
Integrate over the single minute you have chosen to get the volume it contributes.
problems.format: total litres; the minute [a,b]; litres in it

problems.html:
[Physics / applied] A particle moves on a line with velocity v(t)=3t2−12t+9v(t)=3t^{2}-12t+9v(t)=3t2−12t+9 (m s−1^{-1}−1) for 0≤t≤30\le t\le 30≤t≤3.

  1. Find the net displacement ∫03v  dt\int_0^3 v\,\,\mathrm{d}t∫03​vdt.

  2. Find the total distance travelled, ∫03∣v∣  dt\int_0^3\left|v\right|\,\,\mathrm{d}t∫03​∣v∣dt.
hints: Net displacement is the integral of velocity; total distance is the integral of its absolute value.
So find where vvv changes sign first — factorise 3t2−12t+93t^2-12t+93t2−12t+9 and locate the root inside [0,3][0,3][0,3].
Then split the interval there, integrate over each piece separately, and either add the results (net) or add their magnitudes (total).
problems.format: net displacement, then total distance

problems.html: (Substitution with a limit change — worked-example anchor.) ▶\blacktriangleright▶ Evaluate ∫02xx2+1  dx\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} x\sqrt{x^{2}+1}\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫02​xx2+1​dx by converting the limits to the new variable.
hints: The factor xxx outside the root is nearly the derivative of what is inside, which is the signal for substitution.
Put u=x2+1u=x^2+1u=x2+1, so x dx=12 dux\,\mathrm{d}x=\tfrac12\,\mathrm{d}uxdx=21​du, and convert the limits: x=0x=0x=0 gives u=1u=1u=1, x=2x=2x=2 gives u=5u=5u=5.
The integral becomes 12∫15u1/2 du\tfrac12\int_1^5 u^{1/2}\,\mathrm{d}u21​∫15​u1/2du, which the power rule finishes.
problems.format: the value of the integral, to 3 d.p.

problems.html: Evaluate ∫03xx+1  dx\displaystyle\int_{0}^{3} x\sqrt{x+1}\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫03​xx+1​dx. (Here the substitution leaves a stray xxx behind — rewrite it in terms of uuu.)
hints: Put u=x+1u=x+1u=x+1; the substitution is simple, but a lone xxx is left behind outside the root.
Deal with it by rewriting that xxx in terms of uuu as well: x=u−1x=u-1x=u−1.
The integrand becomes (u−1)u=u3/2−u1/2(u-1)\sqrt{u}=u^{3/2}-u^{1/2}(u−1)u​=u3/2−u1/2, two power-rule terms. Change the limits to u=1u=1u=1 and u=4u=4u=4.
problems.format: the value of the integral, as a fraction

problems.html: ▶\blacktriangleright▶ Evaluate two integrals, contrasting the methods: (a) by the f′/f pattern, ∫tan⁡x  dx,(b) by substitution, ∫12ln⁡xx  dx.\text{(a)}\ \text{by the }f'/f\text{ pattern,}\ \int\tan x\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ \text{by substitution,}\ \int_{1}^{2}\frac{\ln x}{x}\,\,\mathrm{d}x .(a) by the f′/f pattern, ∫tanxdx,(b) by substitution, ∫12​xlnx​dx.
hints: In (a) write tan⁡x\tan xtanx as sin⁡xcos⁡x\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}cosxsinx​ and look at which function is the derivative of which.
The numerator is the negative of the derivative of the denominator, so the answer is a logarithm with a minus sign in front.
In (b) substitute u=ln⁡xu=\ln xu=lnx, so du=dxx\mathrm{d}u=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{x}du=xdx​ — the rest of the integrand is exactly uuu. Convert the limits to u=0u=0u=0 and u=ln⁡2u=\ln2u=ln2.
problems.format: the value of (b), to 2 d.p.

problems.html: ▶\blacktriangleright▶ By completing the square, evaluate ∫ dxx2+2x+2\displaystyle\int\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{x^{2}+2x+2}∫x2+2x+2dx​.
hints: The denominator does not factorise, so completing the square is the way in.
x2+2x+2=(x+1)2+1x^2+2x+2=(x+1)^2+1x2+2x+2=(x+1)2+1, which matches the arctangent pattern with a=1a=1a=1.
Substituting u=x+1u=x+1u=x+1 leaves ∫duu2+1\int\dfrac{\mathrm{d}u}{u^2+1}∫u2+1du​ exactly. Remember to convert back to xxx at the end.
problems.format: the antiderivative at x = 0 (C = 0), to 3 d.p.

problems.html:
[Data science / probability] A continuous random variable XXX has probability density f(x)=k x(1−x)f(x)=k\,x(1-x)f(x)=kx(1−x) on [0,1][0,1][0,1] and f(x)=0f(x)=0f(x)=0 elsewhere. A density must satisfy ∫01f=1\int_{0}^{1} f=1∫01​f=1, and P(X≤c)=∫0cf\mathbb{P}(X\le c)=\int_{0}^{c} fP(X≤c)=∫0c​f (probability is area).

  1. Find kkk.

  2. Find P ⁣(X≤12)\mathbb{P}\!\left(X\le\tfrac12\right)P(X≤21​) and comment on the answer.
hints: A density must enclose total area 111, so impose ∫01f=1\int_0^1 f=1∫01​f=1 and solve for kkk.
Expand kx(1−x)kx(1-x)kx(1−x) into kx−kx2kx-kx^2kx−kx2 before integrating; the constant kkk comes outside.
For (b) integrate the same density from 000 to 12\tfrac1221​. The density is symmetric about 12\tfrac1221​, so the answer should not be a surprise.
problems.format: k, then P(X ≤ ½)

problems.html: [Mathematics / pure] ▶\blacktriangleright▶ Let g(x)=∫0x2cos⁡t  dtg(x)=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{x^{2}}\cos t\,\,\mathrm{d}tg(x)=∫0x2​costdt. Find g′(x)g'(x)g′(x) in two different ways and check they agree.
hints: The upper limit is x2x^2x2, not xxx, so the first part of the fundamental theorem needs the chain rule alongside it.
Evaluate the integrand at the upper limit and multiply by the derivative of that limit.
For the second route, integrate cos⁡t\cos tcost explicitly to get sin⁡(x2)\sin(x^2)sin(x2), then differentiate it — the two answers must agree.
problems.format: the value of g′(1), to 3 d.p.

problems.html: [Mathematics / pure] ▶\blacktriangleright▶ Let fff be continuous on [−a,a][-a,a][−a,a]. Using the substitution u=−xu=-xu=−x on ∫−a0f\int_{-a}^{0} f∫−a0​f, prove that ∫−aaf(x)  dx=0\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)\,\,\mathrm{d}x=0∫−aa​f(x)dx=0 whenever fff is odd, and that it equals 2∫0af(x)  dx2\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,\,\mathrm{d}x2∫0a​f(x)dx whenever fff is even.
hints: Split the integral at zero: ∫−aa=∫−a0+∫0a\int_{-a}^{a}=\int_{-a}^{0}+\int_{0}^{a}∫−aa​=∫−a0​+∫0a​, and work on the first piece.
Substitute u=−xu=-xu=−x in that first piece; the limits swap and dx=−du\mathrm{d}x=-\mathrm{d}udx=−du, which flips them back.
You are left with ∫0af(−u) du\int_0^a f(-u)\,\mathrm{d}u∫0a​f(−u)du. Now use the parity of fff: for an odd function this cancels the second piece, for an even one it doubles it.
problems.format: the integral of an odd f over [−a,a]

problems.html:
(Spot the error / conceptual.)

  1. A student writes ∫−11 dxx2=[−1x]−11=(−1)−(1)=−2.\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{x^{2}}=\Bigl[-\frac1x\Bigr]_{-1}^{1} =(-1)-(1)=-2.∫−11​x2dx​=[−x1​]−11​=(−1)−(1)=−2. The integrand is positive everywhere it is defined, so a negative “area” is impossible. What went wrong?

  2. True or false: “∫abf(x)  dx\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫ab​f(x)dx is a function of xxx.” Justify.
hints: The second part of the fundamental theorem has a hypothesis, and the student's calculation quietly ignores it.
Check whether the integrand is continuous everywhere on the interval of integration — look at what happens at x=0x=0x=0.
For (b), ask what kind of object a definite integral is once the limits are fixed numbers: does anything in it still depend on the variable of integration?
problems.format: part (b): true or false

problems.html: Find (a)∫(4x3−6x2+1) dx,  (b)∫(2x3+5x) dx,  (c)∫(e−x+11+x2) dx,  (d)∫(3sin⁡x−4sec⁡2x) dx.\text{(a)}\int\bigl(4x^{3}-6x^{2}+1\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}x,\;\allowbreak \text{(b)}\int\Bigl(\tfrac{2}{x^{3}}+5\sqrt{x}\Bigr)\,\mathrm{d}x,\;\allowbreak \text{(c)}\int\Bigl(\mathrm{e}^{-x}+\tfrac{1}{1+x^{2}}\Bigr)\,\mathrm{d}x,\;\allowbreak \text{(d)}\int\bigl(3\sin x-4\sec^{2}x\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}x.(a)∫(4x3−6x2+1)dx,(b)∫(x32​+5x​)dx,(c)∫(e−x+1+x21​)dx,(d)∫(3sinx−4sec2x)dx.
hints: Every part is term-by-term integration; rewrite any roots or reciprocals as powers first.
In (b), 2x3\dfrac{2}{x^3}x32​ is 2x−32x^{-3}2x−3 and 5x5\sqrt x5x​ is 5x1/25x^{1/2}5x1/2, so the power rule handles both.
In (c) and (d) recognise the standard integrals: 11+x2\dfrac{1}{1+x^2}1+x21​ gives arctan⁡\arctanarctan, and sec⁡2x\sec^2 xsec2x gives tan⁡x\tan xtanx.
problems.format: (a) exact; then (b) at x = 1 (C = 0), 3 d.p.

problems.html: Evaluate (a)∫12 dxx2,  (b)∫0ln⁡2ex dx,  (c)∫0π/4sec⁡2x  dx,  (d)∫−11(x3+x) dx,  (e)∫04x  dx.\text{(a)}\int_{1}^{2}\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{x^{2}},\;\allowbreak \text{(b)}\int_{0}^{\ln 2}\mathrm{e}^{x}\,\mathrm{d}x,\;\allowbreak \text{(c)}\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\sec^{2}x\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\;\allowbreak \text{(d)}\int_{-1}^{1}\bigl(x^{3}+x\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}x,\;\allowbreak \text{(e)}\int_{0}^{4}\sqrt{x}\,\,\mathrm{d}x.(a)∫12​x2dx​,(b)∫0ln2​exdx,(c)∫0π/4​sec2xdx,(d)∫−11​(x3+x)dx,(e)∫04​x​dx.
hints: Antidifferentiate, then subtract the value at the lower limit from the value at the upper.
In (b) the upper limit is ln⁡2\ln 2ln2, and eln⁡2=2\mathrm{e}^{\ln 2}=2eln2=2 — the logarithm and the exponential undo one another.
In (d) the integrand is odd and the interval symmetric, so you can write the answer down without integrating at all.
problems.format: (a)–(e), comma-separated

problems.html: Integrate (a)∫x2(x3+1)7 dx,  (b)∫sin⁡4xcos⁡x  dx,  (c)∫(ln⁡x)2x dx,  (d)∫x e−x2 dx.\text{(a)}\int x^{2}(x^{3}+1)^{7}\,\mathrm{d}x,\;\allowbreak \text{(b)}\int\sin^{4}x\cos x\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\;\allowbreak \text{(c)}\int\frac{(\ln x)^{2}}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x,\;\allowbreak \text{(d)}\int x\,\mathrm{e}^{-x^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x.(a)∫x2(x3+1)7dx,(b)∫sin4xcosxdx,(c)∫x(lnx)2​dx,(d)∫xe−x2dx.
hints: In each case identify the inner function and check that its derivative is present, up to a constant factor.
In (a) take u=x3+1u=x^3+1u=x3+1, whose derivative is 3x23x^23x2 — the integrand has only x2x^2x2, so a 13\tfrac1331​ appears out front.
In (c) the substitution is u=ln⁡xu=\ln xu=lnx, since 1x\dfrac{1}{x}x1​ is exactly its derivative; in (d) it is u=−x2u=-x^2u=−x2, whose derivative supplies the −2x-2x−2x.
problems.format: the constant in front of each of (a)–(d)

problems.html: Evaluate (a)∫12ln⁡xx dx,  (b)∫0π/2sin⁡xcos⁡x  dx,  (c)∫01x(1+x2)2 dx,  (d)∫012xx2+1 dx.\text{(a)}\int_{1}^{2}\frac{\ln x}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x,\;\allowbreak \text{(b)}\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin x\cos x\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\;\allowbreak \text{(c)}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{x}{(1+x^{2})^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x,\;\allowbreak \text{(d)}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{2x}{x^{2}+1}\,\mathrm{d}x.(a)∫12​xlnx​dx,(b)∫0π/2​sinxcosxdx,(c)∫01​(1+x2)2x​dx,(d)∫01​x2+12x​dx.
hints: Each of these is a substitution, and being definite integrals you should change the limits rather than converting back.
In (b) take u=sin⁡xu=\sin xu=sinx; the limits become u=0u=0u=0 and u=1u=1u=1, which makes the arithmetic trivial.
In (c) take u=1+x2u=1+x^2u=1+x2, so x dx=12 dux\,\mathrm{d}x=\tfrac12\,\mathrm{d}uxdx=21​du and the integrand becomes a negative power of uuu.
problems.format: the exact values of (b) and (c)

problems.html: Integrate (a)∫3x2+2x3+2x+1 dx,(b)∫sec⁡2xtan⁡x dx.\text{(a)}\int\frac{3x^{2}+2}{x^{3}+2x+1}\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\int\frac{\sec^{2}x}{\tan x}\,\mathrm{d}x.(a)∫x3+2x+13x2+2​dx,(b)∫tanxsec2x​dx.
hints: Both are the f′/ff'/ff′/f pattern, so the answer is a logarithm in each case — no substitution formalities needed.
In (a) differentiate the denominator and compare with the numerator: they should match exactly.
In (b) rewrite sec⁡2x\sec^2xsec2x as the derivative of tan⁡x\tan xtanx; the integrand is then the derivative of the denominator over the denominator.
problems.format: (a) at x = 1 (C = 0), to 3 d.p.

problems.html: Evaluate the definite integrals (a)∫03 dx1+x2,(b)∫01 dx4−x2,(c)∫02 dx4+x2.\text{(a)}\int_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{1+x^{2}},\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{\sqrt{4-x^{2}}},\qquad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\int_{0}^{2}\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{4+x^{2}} .(a)∫03​​1+x2dx​,(b)∫01​4−x2​dx​,(c)∫02​4+x2dx​.
hints: Each matches one of the inverse-trigonometric standard forms; identify aaa before integrating.
In (a), a=1a=1a=1 so the antiderivative is arctan⁡x\arctan xarctanx; you then need the angle whose tangent is 3\sqrt33​.
In (b), a=2a=2a=2 and the form is arcsin⁡x2\arcsin\tfrac{x}{2}arcsin2x​; in (c), a=2a=2a=2 again but with the arctangent form, which carries a 1a\tfrac1aa1​ out front.
problems.format: the three values; write π as pi

problems.html: Find ∫xx+4  dx\displaystyle\int\frac{x}{\sqrt{x+4}}\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫x+4​x​dx.
hints: Substitute u=x+4u=x+4u=x+4, so du=dx\mathrm{d}u=\mathrm{d}xdu=dx — but a lone xxx remains in the numerator.
Rewrite it as x=u−4x=u-4x=u−4, so the integrand becomes u−4u\dfrac{u-4}{\sqrt u}u​u−4​.
Split that into u1/2−4u−1/2u^{1/2}-4u^{-1/2}u1/2−4u−1/2 and apply the power rule to each, then substitute back.
problems.format: the antiderivative at x = 0 (C = 0), to 3 d.p.

problems.html:
For each function find both the net signed area and the total (painted) area over the stated interval.

  1. sin⁡x\sin xsinx on [0,2π][0,2\pi][0,2π].

  2. x2−1x^{2}-1x2−1 on [0,2][0,2][0,2].
hints: Find where the integrand changes sign first — that is what separates the two calculations.
The net area is one integral over the whole interval; the total area needs the interval split at each crossing.
For the total, integrate over each piece and add the magnitudes, so that the parts below the axis count positively.
problems.format: (a) net, total; then (b) net, total

problems.html: Find the positive value of aaa for which ∫0a(2x+1)  dx=12\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}(2x+1)\,\,\mathrm{d}x=12∫0a​(2x+1)dx=12.
hints: Integrate with the upper limit left as the unknown aaa; the fundamental theorem gives an expression in aaa.
You should reach a2+aa^2+aa2+a, so setting it equal to 121212 gives a quadratic.
Solve it and discard the negative root, since the question asks for the positive value.
problems.format: the positive value of a

problems.html: [Physics / applied] A spring obeys Hooke’s law with force F(x)=kxF(x)=kxF(x)=kx (k=200 N m−1k=200\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}k=200 Nm−1), where xxx is the extension. The work done stretching it from x=0x=0x=0 to x=dx=dx=d is W=∫0dF(x)  dxW=\int_0^d F(x)\,\,\mathrm{d}xW=∫0d​F(x)dx. Find the work to stretch the spring by 0.1 m0.1\ \mathrm{m}0.1 m.
hints: Work is the integral of force over the displacement, so substitute the given FFF and the given limits.
The integrand is 200x200x200x, whose antiderivative is 100x2100x^2100x2.
Evaluate between 000 and 0.10.10.1 — and note the answer is the area of a triangle under the force–extension line, which is a useful check.
problems.format: the work done, in joules

problems.html:
[Data science / probability] XXX has the triangular density f(x)=12xf(x)=\tfrac12 xf(x)=21​x on [0,2][0,2][0,2] (and 000 elsewhere).

  1. Verify it is a valid density.

  2. Find P(X≤1)\mathbb{P}(X\le 1)P(X≤1) as an area.
hints: A valid density needs two things: it must be non-negative, and its total area must be exactly 111.
Check both by integrating 12x\tfrac12 x21​x across [0,2][0,2][0,2] and looking at the sign of the integrand there.
For (b) integrate the same density from 000 to 111; the region is a triangle, so you can check the answer geometrically.
problems.format: the value of P(X ≤ 1)

problems.html: Use FTC Part 1 together with the chain rule to differentiate (a)  d dx∫0x2et  dt,(b)  d dx∫xx2ln⁡(1+t2)  dt.\text{(a)}\ \frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}x}\int_{0}^{x^{2}}\mathrm{e}^{t}\,\,\mathrm{d}t,\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ \frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}x}\int_{x}^{x^{2}}\ln\bigl(1+t^{2}\bigr)\,\,\mathrm{d}t .(a) dxd​∫0x2​etdt,(b) dxd​∫xx2​ln(1+t2)dt.
hints: Both need the first part of the fundamental theorem together with the chain rule, since the limits are not simply xxx.
In (a) the upper limit is x2x^2x2, so evaluate the integrand there and multiply by the derivative of x2x^2x2.
In (b) both limits vary. Split it at any convenient constant so that each piece has one fixed limit, and remember the lower-limit contribution enters with a minus sign.
problems.format: each derivative at x = 1, to 3 d.p.

problems.html: A linear numerator over an irreducible quadratic splits into a logarithm plus an arctangent. Evaluate ∫x+1x2+4x+5  dx\displaystyle\int\frac{x+1}{x^{2}+4x+5}\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫x2+4x+5x+1​dx. (Hint: complete the square below, and write the numerator as a multiple of the denominator’s derivative plus a constant.)
hints: Complete the square in the denominator first: x2+4x+5=(x+2)2+1x^2+4x+5=(x+2)^2+1x2+4x+5=(x+2)2+1.
Now split the numerator: write x+1x+1x+1 as a multiple of the denominator's derivative 2x+42x+42x+4, plus a leftover constant.
The first piece is an f′/ff'/ff′/f logarithm and the second is an arctangent — two standard forms rather than one hard one.
problems.format: the antiderivative at x = 0 (C = 0), to 3 d.p.

problems.html: Evaluate ∫x3x2+1  dx\displaystyle\int\frac{x^{3}}{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫x2+1​x3​dx. (Hint: u=x2+1u=x^{2}+1u=x2+1, and write x3=x2⋅xx^{3}=x^{2}\cdot xx3=x2⋅x.)
hints: Take the hint: u=x2+1u=x^2+1u=x2+1, and split x3x^3x3 as x2⋅xx^2\cdot xx2⋅x so that the lone xxx pairs with dx\mathrm{d}xdx.
Then x dx=12 dux\,\mathrm{d}x=\tfrac12\,\mathrm{d}uxdx=21​du and the remaining x2x^2x2 becomes u−1u-1u−1.
The integral turns into 12∫u−1u du\tfrac12\int\dfrac{u-1}{\sqrt u}\,\mathrm{d}u21​∫u​u−1​du, which splits into two power-rule terms.
problems.format: the antiderivative at x = 0, with C = 0

problems.html: (Spot the error.) A student evaluates ∫0π/2sin⁡2x cos⁡x  dx\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin^{2}x\,\cos x\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫0π/2​sin2xcosxdx thus: “set u=sin⁡x; ∫0π/2u2  du=[13u3]0π/2=13(π2)3.”\text{``set }u=\sin x;\ \int_{0}^{\pi/2} u^{2}\,\,\mathrm{d}u =\Bigl[\tfrac13 u^{3}\Bigr]_{0}^{\pi/2}=\tfrac13\Bigl(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\Bigr)^{3}.\text{''}“set u=sinx; ∫0π/2​u2du=[31​u3]0π/2​=31​(2π​)3.” Identify both mistakes and give the correct value.
hints: Check the substitution itself first — u=sin⁡xu=\sin xu=sinx with du=cos⁡x dx\mathrm{d}u=\cos x\,\mathrm{d}xdu=cosxdx is actually correct.
The trouble is what happened to the limits: they were written in xxx but the integral was then evaluated in uuu.
Convert them properly, x=0x=0x=0 giving u=0u=0u=0 and x=π2x=\tfrac\pi2x=2π​ giving u=1u=1u=1 — or else substitute back to xxx before evaluating. Either repair fixes both errors at once.
problems.format: the correct value of the integral

problems.html:
[Data science / numerical] The integral ∫01e−x2  dx\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{e}^{-x^{2}}\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫01​e−x2dx has no elementary antiderivative (it gives a value of the error function).

  1. Explain why no FTC 2 “plug-in” will evaluate it exactly.

  2. Bracket its value using left- and right-endpoint Riemann sums with n=2n=2n=2 (Δx=12\Delta x=\tfrac12Δx=21​). Is the true value inside your bracket?
hints: For (a), the second part of the fundamental theorem needs a closed-form antiderivative to substitute into — and here none exists in elementary terms.
That does not mean no antiderivative exists: the first part guarantees the area function is one. It simply cannot be written with the usual functions.

For (b) use δx=12\delta x=\tfrac12δx=21​ with heights at x=0,12x=0,\tfrac12x=0,21​ for one sum and x=12,1x=\tfrac12,1x=21​,1 for the other. Since the integrand is decreasing, the left sum overshoots and the right sum undershoots.
problems.format: the bracket: lower then upper, to 3 d.p.

questions.stem: Is ∫01t2 dt\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} t^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t∫01​t2dt a function of ttt?
options: Yes — it depends on ttt through the integrand.
No — it is a function of xxx instead.
No: once the limits are numbers the result is a number, and ttt is only a dummy variable.
Yes, but only because the integrand is a polynomial.
questions.hint: Rename ttt to xxx everywhere in the integral and see whether the value changes.
questions.why: By the time the integration is done, ttt has been used up: nothing in the answer depends on it. Renaming it changes nothing, so ∫01t2 dt=∫01x2 dx=13\int_0^1 t^2\,\mathrm{d}t=\int_0^1 x^2\,\mathrm{d}x=\tfrac13∫01​t2dt=∫01​x2dx=31​. A definite integral depends only on the integrand and its two limits. An integral whose upper limit is itself a variable, such as ∫0xf(t) dt\int_0^x f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t∫0x​f(t)dt, is a different object altogether: that one really is a function — of xxx, not of ttt.

questions.stem: ∫02(x−1) dx=0\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2}(x-1)\,\mathrm{d}x=0∫02​(x−1)dx=0. Does that mean the region between the line and the axis has no area?
options: No: the integral reports net signed area, and here equal areas above and below the axis cancel.
No: the integral vanishes because the line never leaves the axis.
Yes — zero area is exactly what the integral reports.
No — the calculation must contain a slip, since an area is never zero.
questions.hint: Sketch y=x−1y=x-1y=x−1 on [0,2][0,2][0,2] and mark which part of the region lies below the axis.
questions.why: The line lies below the axis on [0,1)[0,1)[0,1) and above it on (1,2](1,2](1,2], and the two triangles are congruent with area 12\tfrac1221​ each. The integral counts the lower one as −12-\tfrac12−21​ and the upper as +12+\tfrac12+21​, so the net is zero while the total painted area is 111. To find total area, locate where the integrand changes sign, split the interval there, and add the magnitudes of the pieces.

questions.stem: A student computes ∫−11dxx2=[−1x]−11=−2\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{x^{2}}=\Bigl[-\frac1x\Bigr]_{-1}^{1}=-2∫−11​x2dx​=[−x1​]−11​=−2, yet the integrand is positive wherever it is defined. What has gone wrong?
options: The antiderivative of x−2x^{-2}x−2 is not −x−1-x^{-1}−x−1.
The integrand is not continuous on [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1], so the fundamental theorem does not apply.
The two limits were substituted in the wrong order.
Nothing — a definite integral is allowed to come out negative.
questions.hint: Check the hypothesis of the theorem being used: is the integrand continuous everywhere on [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1]?
questions.why: The integrand blows up at x=0x=0x=0, which lies inside the interval of integration, so the hypothesis of the second part of the fundamental theorem fails and the bracket calculation means nothing. A negative answer for a positive integrand is the tell-tale that something upstream is wrong. Both the antiderivative and the order of substitution are in fact correct — the fault is in applying the theorem at all. Treated properly as an improper integral, this one diverges.

questions.stem: Substituting u=sin⁡xu=\sin xu=sinx into ∫0π/2sin⁡2x cos⁡x dx\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin^{2}x\,\cos x\,\mathrm{d}x∫0π/2​sin2xcosxdx, what should happen to the limits?
options: They become 000 and 111, the values of uuu at the old limits.
They should be dropped, and the integral treated as an indefinite one.
They stay 000 and π2\tfrac{\pi}{2}2π​ — only the name of the variable has changed.
They become 000 and π2\tfrac{\pi}{2}2π​ multiplied by cos⁡x\cos xcosx.
questions.hint: The limits belong to the variable, and the variable has changed. Work out uuu when x=0x=0x=0 and when x=π2x=\tfrac{\pi}{2}x=2π​.
questions.why: Substitution replaces the variable, and the limits belong to the variable: x=0x=0x=0 gives u=0u=0u=0 and x=π2x=\tfrac{\pi}{2}x=2π​ gives u=1u=1u=1, so the integral becomes ∫01u2 du=13\int_0^1 u^2\,\mathrm{d}u=\tfrac13∫01​u2du=31​. Keeping the old limits while writing the integrand in uuu mixes two variables in one expression and yields nonsense — here 13(π2)3\tfrac13\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)^331​(2π​)3. The alternative route is equally valid: substitute back to xxx first, then use the original limits.

questions.stem: e−x2\mathrm{e}^{-x^{2}}e−x2 has no elementary antiderivative. Does it have an antiderivative at all?
options: Yes, but only for x>0x>0x>0.
Only on intervals where the function is positive.
Yes: the first part of the fundamental theorem makes its area function one — it simply cannot be written with the usual functions.
No — that is precisely what having no elementary antiderivative means.
questions.hint: Distinguish 'exists' from 'can be written down'. What does the first part of the fundamental theorem hand you for any continuous integrand?
questions.why: The integrand is continuous, so F(x)=∫0xe−t2 dtF(x)=\int_0^x \mathrm{e}^{-t^2}\,\mathrm{d}tF(x)=∫0x​e−t2dt is differentiable with F′(x)=e−x2F'(x)=\mathrm{e}^{-x^2}F′(x)=e−x2: an antiderivative, guaranteed to exist on the whole real line. What Liouville's theorem denies is a closed form built from polynomials, roots, exponentials, logarithms and trigonometric functions. The consequence is practical rather than philosophical — the second part of the fundamental theorem has nothing to substitute into, so such integrals are evaluated numerically instead.

questions.stem: What is ddx∫0x2cos⁡t dt\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{x^{2}}\cos t\,\mathrm{d}tdxd​∫0x2​costdt?
options: sin⁡(x2)\sin(x^{2})sin(x2)
cos⁡(x2)\cos(x^{2})cos(x2)
cos⁡x\cos xcosx
2xcos⁡(x2)2x\cos(x^{2})2xcos(x2)
questions.hint: The upper limit is x2x^2x2, not xxx. Ask what the chain rule contributes on top of the fundamental theorem.
questions.why: The first part of the fundamental theorem returns the integrand evaluated at the upper limit — but only when that limit is xxx itself. Here it is x2x^2x2, so the chain rule contributes the derivative of the limit as an extra factor, giving cos⁡(x2)⋅2x\cos(x^2)\cdot 2xcos(x2)⋅2x. The first option is exactly what you get by forgetting it. You can check the answer directly in this case: the integral evaluates to sin⁡(x2)\sin(x^2)sin(x2), whose derivative is 2xcos⁡(x2)2x\cos(x^2)2xcos(x2).
